source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives, Table 2 and text (full PDF read)
finding: Models pick the right narrative well when the analogy also looks similar on the surface, and fail when the analogy is far and the wrong answer looks similar. The hard cell is a far analogy against a near distractor.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy, random 50%, 1,096 triples. Columns: near analogy vs far distractor / near vs near / far vs far / far analogy vs near distractor. GPT-4: 94.0 / 92.5 / 57.1 / 29.1, average 68.1. GPT-3.5: 88.1 / 81.3 / 50.4 / 21.7, average 60.3. SBERT: 84.3 / 71.5 / 12.6 / 1.0. Mean of 9 systems: 76.9 / 73.2 / 45.3 / 33.9. Humans: 98.6 / 97.2 / 96.8 / 91.4, average 96.0.
quote: models only achieved 39.6% on average (worse than random performance) when solving far analogies
limits: Far items are built from shared proverbs, so the far-vs-near cell is partly an adversarial surface lure. Models are GPT-3.5, GPT-4 (2023) and open models; no 2025 reasoning model. Human sample size not recovered from the text I read.
agent_relevance: K08 must be restated: far analogy does not fail by itself, it fails when a surface-similar wrong answer is present. A structure-first check should be tested on exactly the far-vs-near cell.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: interpretation of the 39.6% headline
finding: The 39.6% figure is not one model on one far-analogy test. It is the mean of two far-analogy cells (45.3 and 33.9) across all nine systems, including SBERT and weak T5 models. GPT-4 alone averages 43.1 on far analogies (57.1 and 29.1).
limits: Arithmetic is mine from the paper's Table 2; the paper states 39.6 and 94.1 in prose. GPT-4 far-vs-far (57.1) is only modestly above the 50% chance level.
agent_relevance: K08 stays true in direction but is overstated as 'below chance for strong models'. For GPT-4 the below-chance part is the near-distractor cell only.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: few-shot and chain-of-thought demonstrations
finding: Giving solved examples helps far analogies but hurts near ones. Chain-of-thought examples that first extract the proverb-level message help far analogies more.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 gained close to 10 absolute points on far analogies with random demonstrations. GPT models gained up to 30 points with CoT demonstrations on far analogies (read from figure text, not a table). Near-analogy accuracy dropped with plain demonstrations. GPT-4 was the most stable.
limits: Only GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2; 3 runs averaged; the far-vs-near demonstration experiment was skipped for GPT-4 for cost. Effect sizes are figure readings quoted in prose.
agent_relevance: The step 'extract the abstract message of each narrative first' is a cheap structure-first operator and the one prompt change in ARN that helps far items. Worth testing on a current model.

source: NewtonBench (2025) Table 2, Vanilla vs Code-Assisted symbolic accuracy, re-read from the HTML tables
finding: Re-reading the table confirms the code-tool effect: it helps weak models and slightly hurts strong ones. GPT-5 average symbolic accuracy goes 75.9 to 73.3 (-2.6). GPT-4.1 goes 5.8 to 18.9 (+13.1).
numbers: Average SA vanilla to code: GPT-4.1-mini 5.1 to 14.7; GPT-4.1 5.8 to 18.9; o4-mini 47.8 to 45.1; GPT-5-mini 53.1 to 48.1; GPT-5 75.9 to 73.3; DeepSeek-V3 8.9 to 13.3; DeepSeek-R1 43.4 to 37.4; QwQ-32B 28.5 to 31.4; Qwen3-235B 30.9 to 33.7; Gemini-2.5-flash 50.6 to 40.9; Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4 to 63.7. Hardest cell (hard law, complex system): GPT-5 40.3 to 38.2; Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7 to 22.2. Means over four runs.
limits: The paper's rule 'SA of 40% or more means the tool hurts' has one exception in the table: Gemini-2.5-pro gains on the hardest cell. Gains for Qwen3-235B and QwQ are small (+2.8, +2.9). Differences of 2 to 3 points sit inside the run standard deviations of single cells.
agent_relevance: K14 is confirmed. The strong-model loss is small (-1.7 to -9.7) and has no cell-level significance test; offer the tool, do not forbid it.

source: NewtonBench (2025) section 4.5, exploration-exploitation analysis
finding: The 'code makes strong models explore less' story rests on one trace-token analysis on two models, and the paper calls it correlational. Gemini-2.5-flash's exploration rate falls sharply when code budget goes from 0 to 1; Qwen3-235B's stays stable.
numbers: Exploration rate = share of exploration words (What if, Alternatively) among exploration plus exploitation words (Confirm, Verify). Code-budget runs on four models: stronger ones (Gemini-2.5-flash, GPT-5-mini) degrade at budget 1, weaker ones improve. GPT-5-mini puts less of its code use into plain calculation than GPT-4.1 and more into function fitting.
quote: These observations are correlational and should be interpreted as suggestive rather than causal.
limits: Footnote: observations are correlational. Reasoning traces were visible for only two models, so GPT-5 itself was not analysed. No forced-exploration or quota condition was run.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: nobody has tested an exploration quota. Our guardrail is a hypothesis, not a replicated fix.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2025) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (PNAS Nexus, published version)
finding: Published version of the Webb 2024 reply. GPT-4 with code execution solves permuted-alphabet letter-string analogies at human level; GPT-4 without code and GPT-4 with chain of thought do not. Disabling the code tool removes the gain.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Humans vs GPT-4+code P=0.92; humans vs GPT-4 P<2e-16; humans vs GPT-4+CoT P=3e-8; GPT-4 vs GPT-4+CoT P=0.004; code vs CoT P=4.4e-5. Control with code disabled: GPT-4 21.7% vs 22.5%, P=0.73. 38% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors.
limits: Numbers differ from the earlier preprint in b20 (P=0.496; 46% alternative-rule errors); use these published ones. GPT-4 era; one task family; the code model is an uncontrolled product variant. The authors note coding is not a human strategy.
agent_relevance: K07 should cite P=0.92 and the code-disabled control. Gives a clean causal design for our agent: same model, tool on and off.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2411.14215, extended version)
finding: Three analogy domains tested against variants. Letter strings: humans stay high on permuted and symbol alphabets, GPT drops. Digit matrices: GPT-4 collapses only when the blank is moved (0.813 to 0.480), not with symbols (0.790). Stories: GPT-4 is biased by answer order and drops more than humans when the correct story is paraphrased.
numbers: Digit matrices GPT-4: original 0.813, alternate blank 0.480, symbols 0.790 (humans roughly constant; 1,550 / 1,000 / 1,000 human samples). Far-analogy stories (18 problems): GPT-4 correct-first 0.89 (16/18), correct-second 0.61 (11/18), total 0.75; humans 1.0, 0.72, 0.86. Paraphrased correct story: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (31/36 to 26/36); humans 0.78 to 0.70 (564/720 to 503/720). Letter-string human samples per data point range 92 to 384.
limits: All models GPT-3, 3.5, 4 (2023 versions). Only 18 story problems, and the authors say the paraphrase gap cannot be tested for significance. The 'human sample' conflict in the critique is trial counts per data point, not people; participant count not resolved.
agent_relevance: Order bias and paraphrase sensitivity are cheap to test in our agent: shuffle candidate order and paraphrase sources; treat any drop as brittleness.

source: Beger et al. (2025) Distinguishing Performance From Competence in Evaluations of Humanlike Abstract Reasoning (ConceptARC, reasoning models, Python tools)
finding: On a benchmark of abstract analogy-like grid concepts, o3 matches or beats humans in text, but Python tools do not help in text and slightly hurt the other two models.
numbers: Output accuracy pass@1, 480 tasks, humans 73.0%. o3 text: low 68.3, medium 77.1, low+tools 67.9, medium+tools 75.6. Claude Sonnet 4 text medium 60.2, with tools 55.0. Gemini 2.5 Pro text medium 66.0, with tools 60.4. Visual: o3 medium 5.6 to 29.2 with tools; Claude 5.2 to 6.9; Gemini 4.2 to 5.8.
limits: Not letter-string; grid concepts. Single pass; repeat runs on a 48-task subset show run-to-run variation. Tools help only where perception is the bottleneck (images), echoing the counting bottleneck in d06.
agent_relevance: Offer a tool where the bottleneck is perception or counting, not where the bottleneck is finding the abstraction.

source: Beger et al. (2025) ConceptARC rule analysis
finding: Right answers hide wrong abstractions. About 27% of o3's and Gemini's correct text answers rested on unintended or incorrect rules, about 19% for Claude, about 7% for humans.
numbers: Two annotators: mean agreement 84.8%, Cohen kappa 0.70. Rules scored for o3 in all settings and for Claude and Gemini at medium effort plus tools. Repeat runs on 48 tasks: rule-label consistency 66.0% to 70.9%.
limits: Manual rule labelling. About 19% of human rules were unusable, so the 7% human figure is a lower-bound style estimate. Visual-mode rule percentages were garbled in my extraction and are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Score the agent's stated analogy rule, not only its final answer; accuracy alone overstates analogy competence in text.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench: Benchmarking the Identification of Abstract and Long-context Analogies (EMNLP 2024)
finding: Picking the analogous story out of four gets harder with story length, and scale stops helping. The human to GPT-4 gap grows from 6.9 points at one sentence to 28.8 at 30 sentences.
numbers: T1 accuracy (random 25%), 1 / 10 / 30 sentences: GPT-4 89.1 / 66.5 / 60.7; GPT-3.5 65.3 / 46.4 / 30.8; Claude 68.2 / 30.2 / 25.9; Human 96.0 / 72.5 / 73.3. 340 human-written analogies, 12 open and 3 proprietary models.
limits: Longer versions of the stories were written by GPT-4 from the one-sentence analogies, which could favour GPT-4; the authors checked by scoring GPT-4 on Claude-written stories and report minimal change. 2024 models only.
agent_relevance: Abstraction over long scenarios is where analogy fails; summarising to a relational skeleton before comparing is the natural fix to test.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench task T2: retrieval from a story bank
finding: Finding the analogous story in a bank of 200 is close to random for the best models, except GPT-4-Turbo on one-sentence stories.
numbers: Precision-recall for top-k (k 1 to 10) over a 200-story bank is near the random baseline for GPT-4-Turbo and Claude in most settings; no human run for T2.
limits: From figure and prose, not a table. Two proprietary models only.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that structure-first retrieval fixes this. Gap 3's second half stays open.

source: Si, Hashimoto & Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap (arXiv 2506.20803)
finding: Blind expert scores of LLM research ideas are higher before execution and fall once experts actually run the ideas. Human ideas keep their scores. The novelty edge disappears.
numbers: 43 experts, about 103 hours each, 19 human ideas and 24 AI ideas (Claude-3.5-Sonnet agent). Ideation novelty human 4.912 vs AI 5.778 (FDR p=0.035). After execution novelty 4.903 vs 4.729 (p=0.586). Drops: AI novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879, overall -1.976; human -0.010, +0.078, -0.052, -0.628. Difference in drops p<0.05 on all four metrics (novelty p=0.025).
limits: NLP ideas only. The post-execution human vs AI difference is not significant at N=43 ideas. Ideas were not made with far-inspiration retrieval.
agent_relevance: Human-judged novelty at the idea stage does not predict outcome. Use execution-based checks for any analogy-sourced idea in our agent.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: iterative planning and search for novelty and diversity
finding: Planning what to retrieve, then retrieving external papers, raises the count of unique novel ideas 3.4 times and wins on an LLM Swiss tournament and a 10-expert panel. Retrieval without planning helped less.
numbers: 170 seed papers. Unique novel ideas 3.4x baseline. Swiss tournament: 619 ideas scored 4 and 2,521 scored 5 for Nova. Human panel of 10 experts, at least two raters per idea, 20 ideas per topic per round: Nova had 37.5% of the top-4 ideas and 17.53% of the worst-4 on overall quality.
limits: Human rating folds feasibility into 'overall quality'; no separate feasibility score. Retrieval is topic-relevant, not deliberately far. Small panel, and the LLM ranking drives the headline.
agent_relevance: Planned retrieval beats unplanned retrieval for diversity, but does not answer whether far inspiration lowers feasibility. Gap 8 stays partly open.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning (ICLR 2024)
finding: Having the model propose and solve analogous problems, then reuse their results, beats IO, CoT and Tree-of-Thought on shortest-path at similar token cost for one layer. It is analogical prompting, not a staged structure-mapping operator.
numbers: Shortest-path optimal rate (0-shot): GPT-4 IO 0.78, CoT 0.76, ToT 0.46, TP 0.88. GPT-3.5 IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, ToT 0.22, TP 0.65. PaLM-2 IO 0.14, CoT 0.24, TP 0.36. Text says 1-layer TP costs about the same tokens as ToT; 2-layer costs more for a small gain.
limits: Graph task where analogous problems are easy to generate. Baselines do not include plain analogical prompting. Token costs shown in a figure, not tabulated; not equal-token against CoT with self-consistency.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to gap 1 found: analogical routing beats CoT at about ToT-level tokens, but nobody compared a staged version (constraints, prune, generalise) with plain analogical prompting.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a Step Back: evoking reasoning via abstraction
finding: A first step that states the high-level principle before solving helps a lot on a weaker model and little on a stronger one. It is the 'abstract generically' step of Nersessian's model, tested alone.
numbers: MMLU Physics / Chemistry: PaLM-2L 66.4 / 70.9, CoT 65.0 / 75.3, Step-Back 73.2 / 81.8. GPT-4 69.4 / 80.9, CoT 82.9 / 85.3, Step-Back 84.5 / 85.6. Error analysis (PaLM-2L, Physics): fixes 20.5% of base errors, introduces 11.9%.
limits: Against GPT-4 CoT the gain is only +1.6 (Physics) and +0.3 (Chemistry), about the size of the reported spreads. 2023 models; no reasoning model.
agent_relevance: The abstraction step may add little for strong reasoning models that already abstract internally; test at equal tokens before adding it as an operator.

source: Nature Communications (2026) Human analogical guidance amplifies LLM performance through cross-domain knowledge activation (historical counterfactual on fluid catalytic cracking; authors not recorded)
finding: A 7B model limited to pre-1936 text via RAG rarely invents fluid catalytic cracking alone. When a human supplies the grain-silo analogy, it succeeds every time. The cross-domain facts were already in its context; guidance redirects attention.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B, 600,000-word pre-1936 corpus, 250 trials. Unguided 2/20 success (10%, 95% CI 1-32%). Grain-silo analogy 20/20 (100%, p<0.001). Stokes' Law used in 0/20 vs 18/20; heat management 18/20 vs 1/20. Steering layer 18 at strength 4.5: 0/20 success and incoherent text; four guidance types under steering all 0/80. Zero anachronistic terms in 250 responses.
limits: One 7B model, one invention, and a human supplies the right source analogy (answer-leaking). The no-analogy CoT and generic-CoT prompts were tested only under steering, so there is no unsteered comparison of analogy vs plain CoT. Baseline successes may be pretraining leakage.
agent_relevance: Source selection, not mapping, is the bottleneck: the model had the right material and did not use it. Supports a far-source retrieval operator, but does not show the model can find the source itself.

source: Kretz & Krawczyk (2014) Expert analogy use in a naturalistic setting: the Dunbar and related numbers as quoted (full text read via Europe PMC)
finding: Numbers behind the 'near for fixes, far for ideas' claim, second-hand but from a full text. In Dunbar's microbiology labs almost all analogies were within domain. Distance depends on audience and domain, so 'distance roughly even' is wrong.
numbers: Dunbar (1995, 1997) microbiology labs: 98% of analogies local or regional (within domain). Saner & Schunn (1999) psychology labs: over 75% within domain. Christensen & Schunn (2007) engineering design: 55% within, 45% outside. Blanchette & Dunbar (2001) political articles for the public: 77% outside-category. Dunbar 1995, 1997 and Blanchette & Dunbar 1997-2001: more than half of analogies had no surface similarity.
limits: Second-hand: I could not open any Dunbar primary paper (no open PDF found; his lab site is gone). The review says goals 'appeared to have no effect on analogical distance' in the political data. Analogy counts per lab not given.
agent_relevance: Correct K02 and K19: in expert labs far analogies are rare; far sources come with a lay audience or a design goal. Do not default our agent to far sources.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Scientific Discovery (sections 4 and 9.2, re-read)
finding: States the purpose-distance claim in one place, citing Dunbar 1997 and 2001. Also records a historian's rejection of an earlier cognitive reconstruction of Kepler.
numbers: No counts. Claim: fixing experimental problems uses sources from highly similar domains; new models or concepts use less similar domains; radically different domains are rare. Kepler: Hanson's abductive reconstruction 'is not a historically adequate account' (Lugg 1985).
quote: Analogies between radically different domains, however, are rare
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not a primary test. Lugg's critique targets Hanson (1958), not Nersessian or Gentner et al.
agent_relevance: Precedent that cognitive reconstructions of discovery have been challenged on historical grounds; the same check should be run on hybrid-model readings of Maxwell. 'Rare for radically different' supports medium-distance sources.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Visualization-of-Thought, ring navigation control (arXiv 2404.03622)
finding: Where a rule shortcut exists (clockwise and counter-clockwise steps collapse to addition and modulus), drawing the state did not help and was slightly worse than plain chain of thought.
numbers: Ring of 12, 200 test instances: GPT-4 CoT 52.5% vs GPT-4 VoT 49.5%.
limits: A 3-point gap at n=200 is not significant (standard error of the difference about 5 points). No token or cost comparison in the paper. GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama3 only.
agent_relevance: Supports 'simulate only when no shortcut', weakly. The token break-even (gap 6) is not measured by anyone I found.

source: Raemaekers (2026) Assessing the Relational Abilities of LLMs and Large Reasoning Models (Behavioral Sciences)
finding: Two reasoning models (gpt-oss) do much better than two Llama models on abstract relational analogies built from nonwords, and the result holds when premise order is shuffled.
numbers: Analogy block accuracy: Llama 3.3 70B 47.31, Llama 3.1 405B 55.19, gpt-oss-20B 83.27, gpt-oss-120B 83.85. Shuffled-order replication: 48.27, 55.39, 77.50, 79.81. 1,364 unique problems.
limits: No human baseline. 'Analogy' here means 'is the relation in premise 1 the same as in premise 2', not mapping across domains. Not counterfactual letter strings.
agent_relevance: First reasoning-model point on analogy-type problems with unfamiliar tokens; it does not settle the Webb vs Lewis dispute.

source: Nersessian (2025) How do scientists think? (Topics in Cognitive Science), self-account of method and reception
finding: Nersessian's own account says historians and philosophers in the early 1970s dismissed analogies and diagrams as mere aids, and that her archival work reversed this. The paper has no counts and no independent replication; a text search of it for critics of the Maxwell reading found none.
numbers: Zero hits for Siegel, Chalmers, Darrigol, overfit, underdetermined across 92,887 characters.
quote: widely dismissed by both philosophers and historians of science as ancillary
limits: Absence in her review is not absence in the literature. Web search quota ran out, so independent Maxwell historiography (Siegel, Darrigol, Chalmers) is unchecked.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open. Treat the Maxwell staging as one author's reading until checked against independent Maxwell historians.

source: StoryAnalogy authors (2023) StoryAnalogy: deriving story-level analogies from LLMs (abstract page only)
finding: A 24,000 story-pair corpus annotated for two kinds of similarity shows that ChatGPT picks the analogous story at about 30% in multiple choice while humans exceed 85%.
numbers: ChatGPT about 30% on multiple choice vs humans over 85%. 24K story pairs.
limits: Abstract only, not the tables; 2023 model; chance rate of the choice format not checked.
agent_relevance: A third source that structural story analogy was weak in 2023 models; says nothing about 2025 reasoning models.
